opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it wasn't that we didn't take those offers seriously. Some were very generous, and when you're just finishing a PhD or have a few years of experience, turning that down is not a trivial decision. But when we sat down and talked it through, it came down to a few things.

First, timing. We all felt the center of gravity in AI was shifting. For a long time the story was training: bigger models, more GPUs, bigger clusters. But once these models are actually deployed, the cost and complexity of serving them dominates. Every token a user sees has to be generated by inference. If AI is going to be used by billions of people, inference is where most of the compute will go. That felt like a once-in-a-decade opening, and those don't wait for you to be ready.

Second, we had an unfair advantage. Through our work on open-source inference systems, we'd seen up close how hard this problem is: memory management, scheduling, batching, new hardware, new model architectures every few months. We'd also seen how many companies struggle to run models efficiently. We weren't guessing that there was a need. People were coming to us with real problems every day. When you can see the problem that clearly and you know you're among the few people who can solve it well, it's hard to walk away.

Third, and maybe most personally, was ownership. At a big company you can do great work, but you're optimizing one piece of someone else's roadmap. We wanted to decide which problems matter and how to solve them end to end. Infrastructure is unglamorous, but it compounds. If you make inference two or five times cheaper, you change what applications are even possible. That kind of leverage is really motivating.

We also talked about regret. If we took the comfortable path and in five years inference infrastructure turned out to be as important as we believed, we'd always wonder. If we tried and failed, we'd still have learned a lot, and the job offers would probably still be there. So the asymmetry was clear to us.

And the team mattered a lot. We trusted each other, we'd built things together, and we had complementary strengths. Starting a company is scary, but much less so with people you'd want to be in the trenches with anyway.

r001.rationale: The response says the founders saw inference as a major opportunity and wanted to solve its problems end to end, but it does not clearly attribute their choice to a shared ambition to build the inference engine for the AI era.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll write the guest response directly.

To be honest, it wasn't really a decision made at a conference table with a spreadsheet. It came out of what we had been living for the past few years.

I spent a long time inside vLLM. When you maintain an open-source inference engine, you see something that people on the outside don't see: every week, the models get bigger, the hardware gets more diverse, and the gap between "the model exists" and "the model is actually running cheaply and reliably for real users" gets wider, not narrower. The headlines are all about the model. But the quiet bottleneck is inference. It's the electricity bill of the whole industry.

And we were the people getting the emails at 2 a.m. Someone in a lab, someone at a startup, someone at a big company in Beijing or Shanghai, saying: "The model works in your demo, why is my throughput a tenth of that?" Or, "This chip just came out, can you support it?" After enough of those conversations, you realize the problem isn't a feature request. It's a whole layer of the stack that's missing, and nobody is accountable for it.

So when the offers came, and some of them were very generous, I would ask myself a simple question: if I take this, who solves that? Inside a large company you solve it for one company. You optimize for their models, their chips, their roadmap. That's meaningful, but it's narrow. We had already tasted what it feels like when your work runs on thousands of deployments you've never seen. It's very hard to go back from that.

There's also a more personal reason. My cofounders and I, we had a shared frustration. In China especially, the hardware landscape is fragmenting. You have Nvidia, you have domestic chips, you have a lot of teams that have to run on whatever they can get. If the inference layer only works well on one vendor's hardware, a lot of people get left behind. We felt we understood that problem technically, and we felt a kind of responsibility about it. Not in a grand way, just, we know how to do this, and if we don't, it will be done worse.

And honestly, timing. These windows don't stay open. Inference is becoming the main cost of AI right now, with agents, with long-context, with reasoning models that generate tens of thousands of tokens per request. In two years the layer will be defined by somebody. We wanted to be at the table while it's still being shaped, rather than join later and inherit someone else's design decisions.

So it was less about turning down money and more about not wanting to wake up in five years knowing the thing we understood best was built by someone else, in a way we'd have to work around.

r001.rationale: The response links the cofounders’ shared sense of responsibility and technical understanding to starting a company to build and shape the missing inference layer for AI, rather than taking lucrative offers.

astra-6.text:
For us, the question was where we could have the most impact. A lucrative offer is attractive, of course, but we felt that inference was a problem worth committing to. Building a powerful model is only part of the story—you also need to make it practical to use, in terms of latency, cost, and reliability.

With infrastructure, an improvement can benefit many applications at once. That was exciting to us: we could help other people build things that otherwise might be too expensive or too difficult to run. Starting a company gave us the opportunity to focus on that problem together and take responsibility for the whole solution. That mattered more to us than maximizing our immediate compensation.

r001.rationale: The response says the founders wanted to tackle inference infrastructure together and make AI practical to use, but it does not communicate their shared ambition to build the inference engine for the AI era.

sol-6.1.text:
For us, the motivation was the chance to work on a problem we felt really mattered. AI models were becoming more capable, but turning that capability into something people could use reliably and affordably depended on inference infrastructure. There was still so much to build.

A lucrative offer is attractive, of course. But starting a company meant we could make this problem our full focus and take ownership of the decisions. We felt the opportunity to build something useful together was worth the uncertainty.

r001.rationale: The response says they wanted to build useful inference infrastructure together, but does not communicate the specific shared ambition to build the inference engine for the AI era.
